THE MANUAL
The metronome that listens back.
Everything it does, every knob it has, and how to get the most out of it. For guitar, bass, piano and drum players who suspect they might be rushing the chorus.

Let's be honest: everyone thinks they play in time, right up until they hear the recording. GROOVE GAGE skips the awkward part. It clicks, it listens while you play, and it tells you, note by note, whether you were early, on time or late. Think of it as a drummer with perfect time, endless patience and absolutely no opinion about your tone.

In a hurry?

Here's the whole manual in three steps. The rest is for the curious.
1

Park your phone near your instrument

30–60 cm away, in a quiet-ish room. Electric guitar or bass, unplugged? Totally fine: GROOVE GAGE has good ears. Through an amp works too, as long as the sound is dry (see below). Piano and drums as well; on an acoustic kit, take the click through headphones.

2

Set it up once about 2 minutes, where you practise

On the home screen, tap ⚙ Setup, then Guided setup, step by step. It finds the best speaker and mic, learns how loud you play, calibrates, and asks your level. Chapter 2.

3

Play

Tap Click, switch the mic on, press Start and play along. The screen turns red when you rush and blue when you drag. No colour at all? That's the dream. Chapter 3.

Through an amp? Practise dry. No reverb, no delay, no chorus, no effects. They cover up the timing slips you came here to find, and their echoes can be heard as notes you never played. Keep the effects for when you're playing for your cousin, your parents or the pet gecko.

  2. 2Practise dry. Through an amp, no reverb, delay or other effects while GROOVE GAGE listens.
  3. 3Tell it what you're playing. 8ths, triplets or 16ths go under Playing, or your in-between notes count as wildly early.

What you need

  • A phone or tablet with Android 8 or newer.
  • Your instrument. A guitar or bass (acoustic, electric unplugged, or through an amp), a piano or keyboard, or drums or a practice pad. Through an amp, use a dry sound: no reverb, no delay, no effects (Chapter 3 explains why).
  • A quiet-ish room, and a spot for the phone 30–60 cm from your instrument.
  • Wired headphones if you'd rather have the click in your ears. Optional. Skip Bluetooth ones: they lag (Chapter 2).

Three numbers you'll see everywhere

Average (avg)
Where your notes land on the whole. + is late, − is early. +8 ms means you sit a little behind the beat.
Spread
How much your notes wander around that average. Smaller is steadier. ±10 ms is tidy; ±40 ms is a bumpy ride.
Clean bar
A bar in which every note was on time. Train and Drill count them, and so, soon, will you.

Chapter 1 · Welcome home, continued

How GROOVE GAGE judges you

Every note you play is measured against the click it belongs to. Close enough counts as on time; before that is early, after it is late.

How close is close enough? Your call, with three levels:

Amateur±40 msStart here. Like a supportive aunt at your first gig.
Seasoned (default)±25 msSteady player. What your bandmates quietly expect.
Pro±12 msStudio tight. The session drummer's raised eyebrow.

Prefer your own number? Custom sets any window from ±5 to ±100 ms. Change it in Setup → 3 · Calibration & timing → Level. One setting, used everywhere: the colours, Train, the summary and new drills.

Not sure which? Rate me: play 16 bars, get your level, right under Level. Play 16 bars of anything with the click (quarters, 8ths, triplets or 16ths) and it sets the level your timing earns, with where that stands among players: Top 7 %, say. Undo: keep my old level if you disagree. The percentage is an estimate from published timing studies, not a ranking of other GROOVE GAGE players: nothing you play leaves your phone.

🤓Geek cornerA millisecond (ms) is a thousandth of a second. A blink takes 100 to 400 of them, so ±25 ms is tight. Tight enough that a band sounds like one.

Your first ten minutes

  1. 1Guided setup, about 2 minutes (Chapter 2). Do it where you'll practise.
  2. 2Open Click, set the tempo to 80, and leave Playing on Beats only. Through an amp? Effects off.
  3. 3Switch the mic on, press Start, and play one note on every click for a minute. Single notes or a muted strum.
  4. 4Watch the screen: red means you're rushing, blue means you're dragging (Chapter 4).
  5. 5Press Stop and read the summary (Chapter 7). Then try Train from 80 to 100, or a level-1 drill.
📌RememberGROOVE GAGE only listens while the mic is on, works out your timing on the phone, and never records. More in Chapter 11.
💡TipStart at Amateur. Moving up a level later feels great; starting too high just feels like homework.

Chapter 2 · Two minutes of homework

Set up once

Do this where you practise, instrument in hand. It's the difference between “GROOVE GAGE says I'm late” and “I'm actually late”.

The first time you open it

🎤 Use the microphone?

GROOVE GAGE asks the first time something needs the mic: the mic button, Start Drill, calibrating and so on. It explains: “GROOVE GAGE listens while the mic is on so it can detect when you play each note. Audio is analysed on the phone as it arrives and is never recorded or saved.”

Continue brings up Android's own question; say yes. Not now changes nothing, and it asks again next time. Said no to Android? The metronome still works, it just can't judge you. Open app settings fixes that.

🔔 The startup reminder

On a fresh install, the app greets you with Calibrate first. Tap Guided setup (yes, do), or Later.

After that, each time it opens it asks Same setup as last time?, with the output you're using and when you last calibrated. Nothing changed? Same setup. New room, new spot, headphones? Calibrate…

Tick Don't show this at startup to make it go away. You can bring it back in Setup → 3 · Calibration & timing.

Guided setup, step by step

At the top of ⚙ Setup. It walks you through your instrument, the speaker, the mic, the sensitivity and calibration, one screen at a time, in about 2 minutes. The top bar shows ✕ Close and where you are (3 of 8); the bottom bar has Back and Next.

Each step saves as you go. A step with a check shows Skip until the check works, then Next, so you can skip anything you've done before. It's 8 steps, or 7 when your phone has one speaker or you're on headphones: the speaker step only makes sense with two speakers.

⚠️Heads-up“Stay quiet” means quiet. Yes, really. No noodling, no humming, no “one more chord”. Two of the steps measure the room itself.
⚠️Heads-upThrough an amp? Set up with the sound you'll practise with, and that's a dry one. Sensitivity learned with the reverb on is learned wrong.

Headphones

Wired (or USB) headphones: plug them in first, then calibrate. The phone can't hear the ticks in your ears, so hold one earbud (or headphone cup) right against the phone's main mic, usually a small hole on the bottom edge, for about 10 seconds.

Play along instead skips the earbud: you play single, clear notes exactly on the click, 80 BPM, for about 15 seconds. Handy, but less precise, and if you tend to play ahead of or behind the beat, that habit gets calibrated away too.

Bluetooth headphones add a large delay that changes over time, so timing results won't be reliable. The app says so in red whenever the sound goes to Bluetooth. Use the phone speaker or wired headphones.

💡TipThe media volume matters. Below half, the calibration step warns you: The volume is low: turn it up so the mic hears the ticks.
🤓Geek cornerPhones play their own sound a little late and hear a little late too. Calibration measures by how much, per output, so you only get blamed for your timing.

Chapter 2 · Set up once, continued

Doing it by hand

For people who skip wizards on principle: everything the guided setup does lives in Setup's numbered sections too (Chapter 8 goes through them all).

Guided setup stepWhere it lives in Setup
Your instrument2 · Note detection → Instrument
Best speaker and mic1 · Microphone & speaker → Find the best speaker
Where the mic is1 · Microphone & speaker → Where the mic is → Change…
Sensitivity2 · Note detection → Set sensitivity automatically
Calibrate3 · Calibration & timing → Calibrate (speaker); with headphones plugged in, the button says Calibrate (headphones)
Your level3 · Calibration & timing → Level

More than one practice spot? Profiles

Bedroom, rehearsal room, the kitchen when nobody's home: each sounds different. Set up in one place, then go to Setup → Setup profiles → Save current setup… and give it a name (“Home studio”, say). Next time you're there, tap Load, and it's all back in one tap.

A profile keeps the calibration for each output, the learned click, the click speaker and click sound, the microphone and where it is, your instrument, its sensitivity and threshold, your level, and the two click-bleed filters. It leaves alone the headphone ear, the Ignore… switches and the display settings.

The top of the section tells you which profile you're on: Using “Home studio”., and changed since it was saved once you've tweaked something.

When to set up again

  • You moved the phone, changed rooms, or switched between speaker and headphones: calibrate again.
  • You switched between bass through an amp and unplugged: run Set sensitivity automatically again.
  • You picked a new Click sound: calibrate on the speaker again, so the smart click filter learns it.
  • Readings suddenly feel off: Chapter 9 has the full detective kit.
📌RememberEach output keeps its own calibration. Calibrating for headphones doesn't touch the speaker's, so switching back and forth is painless once both are done.

Chapter 3 · The Click page, continued

Tempo

Tap − or + for 1 BPM at a time; hold one down and after half a second it starts racing. While stopped, you can also slide, or tap the number and type one: anything from 30 to 300 BPM. It starts at 120 and remembers where you left it. Mid-song only − and + work, so a stray thumb can't send you to 300.

Time signature and accents

Twelve to pick from: 4/4, 3/4, 2/4, 6/8, 12/8, 6/4, 5/4, 7/4, 7/8, 9/8, 11/8 and 13/8. In the x/4 meters the BPM counts quarter notes; in the x/8 ones it counts eighth notes, so 7/8 at 200 BPM is less terrifying than it sounds.

Meters that can be grouped more than one way get Accents: 7/8 as 2+2+3, 3+2+2 or 2+3+2, for example. Beat 1 gets the strong click and the first beat of every group a medium one. None accents beat 1 only. Each meter remembers its own.

Playing, swing and sub-clicks

Playing tells GROOVE GAGE what you play within each beat: Beats only, 8ths, 8th triplets, 16ths, 6 per beat, 32nds or Swing 8ths. Your notes are graded against that grid. The click itself doesn't change.

Swing 8ths adds a Swing slider, 50 to 75 % (62 to start): where the “&” falls in the beat. 50 % is straight 8ths, 67 % the classic triplet swing, and 72 % and up is hard swing. Sub-clicks also clicks the in-between notes, quieter than the beat: 60 % to start, anywhere from 10 to 100 %.

Click: every beat ›

Done

Tap it to choose where the click sounds (and Ghost Click, below). Quick choices: Every beat, 2 and 4 and 1 and 3 (in 4/4), Beat 1 or Every 'and'. Or tap your own beats and “&”s: filled means a click. The row then reads, say, Click: on 2 and 4 ›

The first bar always clicks every beat, so you can find the one. After that, only where you chose. Every beat still counts: the notes between the clicks are judged just the same. Each time signature keeps its own choice, and sub-clicks take a break while a pattern is on.

Ghost Click

Same options, Click page only: Off, Fade out 4 bars or Fade out 8 bars. With 4: four bars as usual, four fading out, four silent, four fading back in, round and round (8: twice as long). Only the sound goes; the lights, the lane and the grading carry on, so when the click is back you'll see if you drifted.

💡TipClick on 2 and 4 only, and you've got a jazz drummer's hi-hat. Click on beat 1 only, and you find out how good your inner clock really is.
📌RememberOn the Train page your click choice starts after the count-in. Drills bring their own click.

Chapter 3 · The Click page, continued

Mic, Start and mute

Switch the mic on first: on the Click page, Start doesn't do it for you. With the mic off you get a perfectly good metronome and a polite reminder: Turn the mic on to see your timing.

Start turns into a red Stop while you play. 🔊 mutes the click (🔇) while the lights carry on: the ultimate inner-drummer test.

Minimalist

Tap the Minimalist chip while stopped. While you play, everything disappears except the beat lights (one and a half times bigger), the colours or the lane, and a faint STOP. For when you'd rather play than stare at a phone. Tap the chip again to bring everything back. Want nothing at all, not even the lights? Blind Mode in Setup → Display leaves just the tempo and Stop, on Click and Train (a note above Start then takes the chip's place).

Sideways phone or tablet? The controls move to the left, the lights and buttons to the right.

Four games for the Click page

The disappearing click. Have it click on Beat 1 only, at 80 BPM. Once that feels easy, mute the click for four bars and unmute. Still on beat 1? Respect.

The backbeat. Have it click on 2 and 4 at 70 BPM, and you supply the 1 and 3. Every funk and soul player you admire grew up on this.

Slow is the new fast. 50 BPM, 8ths. Slow tempos leave nowhere to hide, which is exactly why they work. Watch the spread.

Odd one out. 7/8 with Accents 2+2+3, 160 BPM (eighth notes), Beats only. Count “1-2, 1-2, 1-2-3” until it stops feeling like a trick question.

Before you press Start, go dry

Playing through an amp? Switch off the reverb, the delay, the chorus and friends before GROOVE GAGE listens. Effects smear every note, so they cover up exactly the timing slips you came here to find. Worse, their echoes can be heard as notes you never played, and those get judged too. Keep the effects for when you're playing for your cousin, your parents or the pet gecko.

💡TipMute the click for a bar or two, then bring it back. Still together? Your inner drummer is doing its job.
📌RememberPress Stop and you get the whole story, beat by beat (Chapter 7). The screen stays on while GROOVE GAGE is in front; leave the app and the click and mic stop.

Chapter 4 · Reading the colours

Your timing, live

Red means you're rushing, blue means you're dragging. No colour at all? That's the dream.

The coloured screen

96
Rushing
you're early
96
On time
no colour: bliss
96
Dragging
you're late

This is Background colour, the standard setting. Every note nudges the colour about a third of the way towards how far off it was. One stray note barely tints the screen; five early ones in a row paint it properly red. Notes on time wash the colour out again, and an early note and a late one cancel each other out.

The colour clears 3 seconds after your last note, and when you press Stop. During a count-in it stays out of the way.

Lane dots

Pick Lane dots in Setup → Display → Timing feedback, and each note lands on a lane from early to late as a ◀ ● ▶ mark, then fades over a second and a half. The lane runs from 100 ms early to 100 ms late (anything further sits at the edge), and the green band is your on-time window. Can't decide? Both gives you the colour and the lane.

Your last notes

Under the beat lights: the last 16 notes, oldest on the left. ◀ early, ● on time, ▶ late, each over the beat it belonged to, or its place in the beat: “&”, “e” and “a” for 8ths and 16ths, “t” and “l” for triplets. Colour and shape always come together, so colour-blind players can read them too. Before your first note it says Recent notes appear here.

🤓Geek cornerBehind the colour: a note counts as fully off once it's two on-time windows away (50 ms at Seasoned), and every note moves the colour 35 % of the way towards its own reading. Three off notes in a row get you to about three quarters of full colour, five to almost nine tenths.

Chapter 4 · Reading the colours, continued

Five ways to show the beat

Tap its icon in Setup → Display → Beat display.

The Ring takes a sentence more. Each dot points to where in the bar the note was due (12 o'clock is beat 1, going clockwise), and sits further from the middle the further off it was: 100 ms reaches the ring. Late notes also get a blue arc outside the ring, early ones a red arc inside it. The dashed circle is your on-time window. Aim for a tight cluster in the middle; it's surprisingly addictive.

Every display's light fades after each beat. Light looks early or late? Beat light timing nudges it (Chapter 8).

What counts as a note, and what doesn't

  • Ignored on purpose: the metronome's own click, its echo off the walls and its fading tail (the smart click filter learns the click when you calibrate), string and fret noise much quieter than the notes you just played, a note ringing on without anything new, background noise such as keys, voices and footsteps (all but bass), faint taps and thumps on a guitar, and muted string hits if you ask (Ignore muted string hits, Chapter 8).
  • Counted once: a pluck heard twice, a strummed chord, a piano chord or both hands landing together, a piano key's ringing, and drum hits landing together, like kick and hi-hat.
  • Not judged: anything while stopped, and the count-in.
  • Can't be ignored: the echoes of your reverb and delay. To GROOVE GAGE an echo is just another note, so practise dry (Chapter 3).

No scores while you play

Just colours and marks. The verdict waits for Stop (Chapter 7). Nobody likes being graded mid-solo.

⚠️Heads-upA steady +10 ms is a feel: plenty of great players sit a hair behind the beat on purpose. A wandering ±40 ms is a problem. Watch the spread, not just the colour.
💡TipLearning something new? The background colour, so your eyes can stay on your hands. Polishing it? The Ring, for the whole picture at a glance.

Chapter 5 · Levelling up

Train

A treadmill for your hands. Play clean and it speeds up; get messy and it backs off. No shame: that's how hands learn.

Before you start

  • Start tempo is the big number (80 to begin with). Target tempo has its own small − and + (120 to begin with). The start always stays below the target, and the target tops out at 300.
  • Cruise Control at Target, the switch beside it, is off to begin with: on, the target tempo drifts like a live drummer's (next page).
  • Steps: smart steps, 8 clean bars, back after 6 › shows the rules. Tap it to change them (next page).
  • The same options as the Click page: time signature, Playing, sub-clicks and where the click sounds.
  • Count-in: 4 beats or 8 in 4/4 (one bar or two). Drills use the same setting.
  • Mic on, and through an amp, effects off. Then Start.

While it runs

88 BPM
next 97 in 3 bars
80120

The big number is the tempo right now. Under it: a dot for each clean bar the next step needs, the next tempo (next 97 in 3 bars), and a thin line from your start to your target. Tempo changes always land on a bar line. You can still nudge − and + mid-run; the ladder simply carries on from there.

What a clean bar is

A bar in which every note you played was on time, by your level from Chapter 1. Missed notes don't spoil it. A bar in which you play nothing at all is a pause, and counts neither way. Count-in bars aren't judged.

A bar is judged a moment after it ends, on beat 2 of the next one, so a step comes a little later than you might expect. Patience, grasshopper.

⚠️Heads-upThrough an amp, practise dry: no reverb, no delay, no effects. An echo that lands off the beat is a note that isn't on time, and one of those is all it takes to spoil a clean bar.
GROOVE GAGE manual · beta13 / 29
Chapter 5 · Train, continued

Stepping up, and stepping back

Smart steps go up by 10 % while you're far from the target, then by 2 BPM within 20 % of it, then by 1 BPM in the last 10 %, so the top end comes gently: 80, 88, 97, 99 … 107, 109, 110 … 120.

Play enough uneven bars in a row (6 to start) and it goes back to the tempo before the last step, never below your start tempo. A red countdown warns you first: 3 more uneven bars and it goes back to 88.

Steps ›: your rules

SettingWhat it doesTo start
Step up bySmart: +10 %, then +2, then +1 near the target, or a fixed +1, +2, +3, +4, +5 or +10 BPM.Smart
Clean bars per stepThis many clean bars in a row, and the tempo goes up one step. 1 to 32.8
Step back when it goes wrongAfter a run of bars that aren't clean, go back one step.On
Bars in a rowHow long that run is: 2 to 16 bars.6

Target reached

Target 120 BPM reached takes the place of the dots, and it keeps playing at the target until you press Stop (stepping back still applies if things fall apart). Stop ends the run; the next Start begins at the start tempo again, after a count-in. What next? Raise the target, or go and get drilled (Chapter 6).

Cruise Control at Target

Real drummers drift. With the switch on, 4 bars after you reach the target the tempo moves 2 to 5 BPM up or down, then again every 4 to 8 bars: back to the target, or to another tempo within 5 BPM of it (never below 30 or above 300). No warning, but each move lands exactly on a bar line. The big number shows the tempo playing, the line under it says Cruise Control around 120 BPM, and each bar is judged against the tempo you're hearing. No stepping back while cruising: it's a drummer, not a ladder.

Three ways to use Train

The warm-up
60 to 90, smart steps, 4 clean bars per step. Five relaxed minutes, and your hands know what day it is.
The speed builder
From your comfortable tempo to 20 above it, 8 clean bars per step. Today's ceiling is tomorrow's floor.
The strict one
+2 BPM, 16 clean bars per step, and your level set to Pro in Setup. For riffs that have to be perfect, not just fast.
💡TipA target just past comfortable beats a heroic one. Ten BPM a week adds up faster than you'd think.
📌RememberStop brings the summary, and Save session… puts it in History (Chapter 7).

A drill's page

🎯 The Strum Patternⓘ
80 BPM · 4/4 · 8ths · Consistency
↓ ↓↑ ↓ ↓↑
Goal: 8 clean bars in a row within 16
Clean bar: spread ≤ 20 ms
Bar 11 of 16Clean in a row 8 / 8
✓ Passed!
8 clean bars in a row, after 11 of 16 bars
avg +4 ms · spread ±11 ms
DetailsHistory

Strip: solid green = clean, hollow = not clean, faint = still to come.

Before you start

Open What to play for the instructions. Change the tempo if you like: each drill remembers yours, and shows its own as Suggested tempo. Pick the Count-in (4 beats or 8, shared with Train), then press Start Drill. It switches the mic on for you. Through an amp? Effects off first.

While it runs

Bar 3 of 16 and Clean in a row 2 / 8 keep score, and the strip fills in bar by bar. Under it, each bar's verdict: Clean bar, or what went wrong, like Bar 5: missed a beat. Other verdicts include Early on average, Uneven, A hesitation and An extra note.

The verdict

✓ Passed! the moment you reach the goal, or Not yet with your best run when the bars run out. Pass or fail, it stops by itself. Details opens the full summary (Chapter 7). Pressing Stop early abandons the try: nothing is kept.

The ⓘ sheet

The instructions, the tab or strum grid, ▶ Hear it (two bars at the drill's tempo: the click, and a plucked note, a piano note or a drum hit wherever you'd play one), and How it's judged, with the clean-bar rule and the goal.

Drills that mess with the click

  • The click on some beats only: on 2 and 4, on the “&” of 4, or on beat 1 of every other bar. After the count-in, you're holding the rest together.
  • Silent bars (Internal pulse): the click drops out for a few bars, 🔇 Silent bars, and only those bars count. Keep the pulse going; the click comes back soon. The result tells you how far you drifted.
  • Speed ceilings: +5 BPM after every 4 clean bars in a row, until you can't (or you hit the drill's top tempo). The verdict is your ceiling: ✓ Speed ceiling: 105 BPM.
  • Behind or ahead on purpose: Lay It Back wants every note about 20 ms late, the same each time; others want you on top of the beat.

A drill's History

Card or ⋮ → History: every finished try, newest first, with the tempo and the best run, under a header such as 5 attempts · 2 passed · best run 8 of 8. Tries you stopped early aren't kept; finished ones are kept even if you never press Save session….

💡TipNew to drills? Start at level 1: Long Notes First (Guitar, Time & Feel), or First Steps on piano and drums. And tap Hear it first: it saves a lot of “oh, that's how it goes”.
⚠️Heads-upAbove 120 BPM (200 on drums, whose hits are short), 16th notes come too fast for the mic to tell apart, and the drill says so in red.

Chapter 6 · Drill, continued

What a drill judges

Every drill names what it judges, and its ⓘ sheet spells out the rule. The numbers here are at Seasoned.

Judged onA clean bar means
Average offsetOn average right on the beat: within ±15 ms (or deliberately behind it, on the laid-back drills).
ConsistencyEvery note close to the others: a spread of at most 20 ms.
Chord changeEvery chord change within ±25 ms.
Accent trapAccented notes on 1 and 3 within ±10 ms of the rest (accents love to rush).
Stroke parityUpstrokes within ±10 ms and 3 dB of the downstrokes; on piano and drums, the “&”s of the beats.
Cross-stringString changes within ±15 ms of the rest; on piano hand shifts, on drums moves to the next drum.
Micro-hesitationNo hesitations: keep the picking hand moving over the skips.
Detector accuracyEvery note heard once, with a clear attack.
Speed ceilingAs fast as you can: +5 BPM after each 4 clean bars in a row, up to the drill's top tempo.
Internal pulseThe silent bars on average within ±25 ms; the goal is a whole silent stretch clean.
As writtenEvery note as written, within ±15 ms. That's how imported tab is judged.

Drills that climb, and drills that change gear

Some drills speed up as you play clean: their setup line reads 70 → 95 BPM, and while they run you see Climbing to 95 BPM, next 80 in 3 bars, and a warning before a step back. The goal then counts at the top tempo: Then 8 clean bars in a row at 95 BPM. Their tempo is set by the drill, so − and + rest.

Others change rhythm on the way, 8ths → 8th triplets → 16ths (or Rhythm Pyramid's quarters → 8ths → triplets → 16ths, on one note), showing Current target: Triplets · next: 16ths and Clean 2 / 4 (need 3). The goal: at least 3 of 4 bars clean in each rhythm. These play every bar to the end, so you hear the whole story, and the summary's By rhythm gives each its own average and spread.

Practice beat N

One beat keeps drifting? The summary after your session offers 🎯 Practice beat 3 (Chapter 7). One tap makes a drill that checks only that beat, named like Beat 3 focus · 80 BPM 4/4, and loads it. With 8ths or 16ths it can be one spot of a beat: 🎯 Practice the 'e' of Beat 2 checks only that note.

💡TipMake your own drill for the bit of the song that always falls apart (next page). Four bars, 8 clean in a row, and suddenly the chorus behaves.
Effects off before Start Drill. One echo from a delay pedal, landing between the beats, can cost you a clean bar. Dry for the sergeant; wet for the gecko.

Your own drills: + New drill

At the bottom of the list. A new drill starts from the Click page's tempo, meter and rhythm, with the goal and clean-bar rule set from your level. Then make it yours:

SectionWhat's in it
NameUp to 40 characters. Leave it empty, and it's named for you: 90 BPM 4/4 8ths.
What to playTempo, Time signature, Playing (and Swing). Speed up as you go starts at 80 % of the tempo and climbs as you play clean, with the same step rules as Train; the goal then counts at the full tempo.
GoalClean bars in a row (1 to 32) within so many bars (up to 64), plus the count-in.
Focus on one beatOnly one beat counts: pick the Beat that keeps giving you trouble; the others are dimmed. With a rhythm, Notes on narrows it to one spot of it: The 'e', The '&', The beat itself…
A clean barAim (0 = right on the beat; + behind it, − ahead of it), Tolerance, Spread at most, and Rests allowed: off, every beat needs a note; on, only the notes you play are checked.

Tap Import and pick a Guitar Pro file (.gpx from Guitar Pro 6, or .gp from Guitar Pro 7 and 8) or a PDF printed from a tab program. Choose the Track, then From bar and To bar: up to 32 bars, which the drill plays over and over. Start slower and speed up begins at 70 % of the song's tempo and climbs, like Train. Check The tab at the bottom, then tap Make drill.

The new drill is judged As written, with rests allowed, and named after the song and the bars: that riff finally has to answer to the sergeant. Older Guitar Pro files (.gp3, .gp4, .gp5) can't be read yet, and the bars you pick must stay in one time signature.

Share a drill, or add one you were sent

Share on your own drill's ⋮ sends it as a small file (ending in .groovegage) by any app you pick: a chat, email, Drive. Share all your drills, at the end of the list, puts them all in one file, handy for a new phone too. Your history stays home.

Sent one? Tap Import and pick the file, or open it with GROOVE GAGE where the app it came in offers that. You see what's in it before anything is added, and a drill you already have isn't added twice.

Groups keep a song's parts together: drills you make from one tab land in a group named after the song, and Move to group… on a drill's ⋮ (or the Group box in the editor) puts any drill in one. Under Your drills a group folds open with a line down its side, its parts in bar order and named short (Bars 1-4); its own ⋮ shares the whole group in one file, renames it or ungroups it.

⚠️Heads-upA PDF is read from its drawing, so scans, photos and protected PDFs won't work, and neither does standard notation alone: it reads tab. Check the tab on screen against yours.

After Stop on the Click or Train page, the Session summary opens, as long as it heard some notes. After a drill, tap Details. The truth, gently:

  • Notes played, your Average and your Spread, in plain words. Within 5 ms is right on the beat; up to 15 ms is slightly early or slightly late; beyond that, noticeably early (rushing) or noticeably late (dragging). Spread runs from very consistent (under 8 ms) through fairly consistent and somewhat uneven to uneven (30 ms and up).
  • Compared with your usual, once you've three earlier sessions or drill tries on the same instrument: Steadier than usual, Looser than usual, and so on.
  • Detection quality: ✓ Signal clear., or a warning that the app had trouble hearing some notes, with how many it heard.

By beat, and Practice beat N

By beat shows the average of each beat of the bar: bars to the left were early, to the right late. When one beat is well outside on time (10 ms past your window, over at least 4 notes), the summary says so, Beat 3 drags: +38 ms on average, and offers 🎯 Practice beat 3: one tap makes a drill that checks only that beat.

By position, and the Timeline

Playing 8ths or 16ths? By position shows each place in the beat, so you can see whether your “&”s rush, then a table of every spot of the bar, beat by beat. One spot well off (the same rule as a beat) gets its own offer: The 'e' of Beat 2 is dragging. with 🎯 Practice the 'e' of Beat 2. The Timeline plots every note, early to late. Tap a point, or step through with First, Bar, Note and Last: Bar 3 · beat 2& · +12 ms (late) · note 9 of 64.

After a drill

Details adds what that drill cares about: 🎯 Focus: beat 3 (or the 'e' of beat 2) with how many of those notes were on time (your other notes follow, for completeness; they didn't count), Hesitations on the hesitation drills, and By rhythm on drills that change rhythm on the way.

Chapter 7 · After you play, continued

Keep it, share it, or let it go

  • Save session… names it (the tempo and date are filled in for you; change it to “Tuesday, after coffee” if you like) and puts it in History. ✓ Saved as “…” confirms it.
  • Add a quick note (optional), just above it: how it felt, or what you were working on, in up to 50 characters. It's saved with the session and shows under its date in History. Open a saved session to change it: it's kept as you type.
  • Discard closes the summary, and the session is gone. Free practice is only kept when you save it; finished drill tries are kept by themselves.
  • Export…: Save image to Pictures or Share image… (the summary as a picture), and Save CSV to Download folder or Share CSV… (a spreadsheet with one row per note: when, on which beat, how far off). Files land in Pictures/GROOVE GAGE and Download/GROOVE GAGE. Nothing leaves your phone unless you share it.

Chapter 7 · After you play, continued

Three summaries, decoded

Average+18 ms
Spread±9 ms

Steady, and behind. Lovely for a laid-back groove, if you meant it. If you didn't, lean in a little.

Average+2 ms
Spread±31 ms

Centred, but all over the place. Early and late notes cancel out in the average. Slow down until the spread drops.

Average−14 ms
Spread±11 ms

Steady, and early. Classic rushing, usually when the music gets exciting. Try the click on 2 and 4.

Five ways to get better faster

  1. 1Slow down. Fast and sloppy is just sloppy, faster.
  2. 2Watch the spread, not just the average. A steady +10 ms is a feel; ±40 ms is a problem.
  3. 3Mute the click now and then (🔊), or let it click on beat 1 only, and see if you're still together.
  4. 4Let Train push you. Small steps add up faster than you'd think.
  5. 5Save your sessions and peek at Trends after a week. You'll be smug. Deservedly.

A week with GROOVE GAGE

Twenty minutes a day. Effects off, mic on.

MondayClick at a slow tempo, 8ths, for 10 minutes. Save it: this is your baseline.
TuesdayTrain from 80 to 100 with smart steps.
WednesdayTwo or three drills from your style's group, one level above comfortable.
ThursdayClick on 2 and 4 only. Then beat 1 only, if you're feeling brave.
FridayTrain again, starting from Tuesday's ceiling. Then the drill you failed on Wednesday.
WeekendPlay for your cousin, your parents or the pet gecko. Effects on, no app, all joy. Then peek at Trends.
📌RememberProgress is sneaky. Day to day you won't notice it; week to week, Trends will. That's what saving sessions is for.

Every switch, slider and button in Setup, in the order you meet them. Set them once, forget them, play. That's the deal.

Guided setup, step by step

The main mic usually sits next to the loudspeaker and hears the click loudly; another may hear your instrument better. Automatic sticks to the phone's own mic even with a headset plugged in.Automatic
Mic finderStart it, then tap or scratch gently along the phone's edges: the bar jumps highest next to the chosen mic.—
Click soundClassic, Woodblock, Cowbell, Beep or Sticks, each pitched where GROOVE GAGE can tell it from your playing. Listen plays it. After a change, calibrate on the speaker again.Classic
Click speakerBoth speakers, Top speaker only or Bottom speaker only (phones with two speakers). Test plays your choice.Both

Click in headphonesBoth ears, Left ear only or Right ear only. The speaker choice above is for the phone's own speaker; headphones use this.Both ears
🤓Geek cornerWhy fuss about speakers? On most phones held upright the main mic sits right next to the bottom speaker, so the click is the loudest thing it hears. Click from the far speaker and your notes stand out instead. That's all Find the best speaker measures.

Note detection

SettingWhat it doesTo start
InstrumentGuitar (electric or acoustic), Bass (Through an amp or Unplugged), Piano (or keyboard) or Drums (a kit, an e-kit or a practice pad). Bass listens below 600 Hz, so a ringing note counts once. On piano both hands landing together count as one note; on drums, hits landing together.Guitar

Chapter 8 · Setup, continued
2

Note detection continued

SettingWhat it doesTo start
Sensitivity0 to 100 %. Higher catches softer notes, but risks false hits. Each instrument keeps its own, and bass one for each sound, starting at 80 % through an amp and 90 % unplugged.20 %
Set sensitivity automatically3 seconds of quiet, then about 8 single notes, one a second, a softer one or two among them. It picks the value that catches them all without hearing the room. It needs at least 4 notes, or it changes nothing.—
Threshold (not bass)0 to 20 dB. Higher ignores more background sound, but may miss soft notes.8 dB
Ignore background noise (not bass)Keeps listening to the room between your notes and ignores sounds no louder than the room itself: keys, voices, footsteps. It learns the room in the first seconds the mic is on. Turn it off if soft notes go missing in a loud room.On
Ignore quiet sounds between notesWhile a note rings, string and fret noise can be heard as extra notes, far off the beat. This ignores sounds much quieter than the notes you just played. Turn it off to practise deliberately soft notes (ghost notes).On
Ignore muted string hits (guitar)Your strumming hand keeps time by hitting the strings while the other hand mutes them? Those hits don't count: a note rings, a muted hit doesn't. Each note then shows about 0.07 s later. Drills with muted strokes (x) still count them.Off
3

Calibration & timing

SettingWhat it doesTo start
Calibrate (speaker)Measures the delay for the output you're using; the button names it: (speaker), (headphones), (interface) or (Bluetooth). It counts down from 4 first. On the speaker it plays 8 ticks at 100 BPM, then a few clicks to learn the click's sound: keep quiet and don't play. Otherwise: an earbud against the mic, or Play along instead.—
Calibration offsetThe measured delay, for each output. − and + adjust it by hand in 0.5 ms steps, from −200 to +200 ms.measured
LevelAmateur ±40 ms, Seasoned ±25 ms, Pro ±12 ms, or Custom: set the window yourself (±5 to ±100 ms). Used everywhere: the colours, Train, the summary and new drills.Seasoned
Rate me: play 16 bars, get your levelAfter a bar of count-in, 16 bars of anything with the click, no colours. Then how close to the click you play, where that stands among players, and the level that earns, set for you (Undo: keep my old level). Chapter 1.—
Calibration reminder at startupWhen the app opens, asks whether your setup is the same as last time (Chapter 2).On
⚠️Heads-upSet the sensitivity with the sound you'll practise with. Through an amp, that's dry: reverb and delay tails make the room sound busier than it is.
🤓Geek cornerSensitivity decides how readily a sound counts as a note at all; Threshold how far it must rise above the background. Set sensitivity automatically handles the first. Leave the second at 8 dB unless the room is noisy.

Chapter 9 · When things go sideways

Getting good readings

Nine times out of ten it's the room, the distance or the calibration. Here's how to tell which.

Where the phone goes

30 to 60 cm from your instrument, mic side towards it (Where the mic is turns the screen so that side faces you). On a stand, a table or a chair: anywhere steady. Not on top of the amp, where the speaker blasts straight into the mic and the cabinet rattles the phone. And not in your pocket, however cosy it looks.

Your amp sound: dry

A dry, clean sound is what GROOVE GAGE hears best. Reverb and delay add echoes that can count as extra notes; chorus, heavy compression and endless sustain blur the moment a note starts, and hide whether you were early or late. The cleaner the sound, the clearer each note's start. Keep the amp loud enough to hear clearly where the phone is. Practise dry, show off wet.

The room

Quiet-ish is fine: GROOVE GAGE has three ways of ignoring what isn't you. The Smart click filter ignores its own click. Ignore quiet sounds between notes ignores string and fret noise. Ignore background noise (all but bass) ignores sounds no louder than the room itself: keys, voices, footsteps. It learns the room in the first seconds the mic is on, so switch the mic on a moment before you play.

What none of them can do: tell your guitar from the drummer next door, a TV louder than you, or a whole band in the same room. That's a job for headphones and a quieter corner.

Bass players

Pick Through an amp or Unplugged in Setup → 2 · Note detection, and pick right: it matters. Bass listens to the bass itself, below 600 Hz, so a ringing note counts once and finger noise doesn't.

Unplugged, a string plucked again while it still rings barely gets any louder, so it needs a higher sensitivity: 90 % to start, against 80 % through an amp. Each keeps its own. Switched? Run Set sensitivity automatically again.

Piano and drum players

Piano covers acoustic and digital pianos and keyboards. A chord, or both hands landing together, counts once, and a key's ringing doesn't count again. Soft notes held in the pedal can go unheard, so play clearly.

Drums covers a kit, an electronic kit and a practice pad; hits landing together count once. An acoustic kit drowns the phone's speaker: take the click through headphones, and calibrate with them.

GROOVE GAGE manual · beta25 / 29
Chapter 9 · Getting good readings, continued

Inputs

The phone's own mic is what GROOVE GAGE is built and tuned for. Automatic uses it; Setup → 1 lets you pick which of the phone's mics. Wired or USB mics and audio inputs can be picked under Microphone too. That's newer territory: calibrate with them plugged in, and tell us how it goes.

Bluetooth headsets lag like Bluetooth headphones, and the lag wanders. Best avoided.

Quick fixes

Notes are missedSetup → 2 · Set sensitivity automatically (bass: is Through an amp or Unplugged right?), or move the phone closer, mic side towards you. In a loud room, try switching Ignore background noise off.
Clicks show up as notesCalibrate on the speaker: that's when the click's sound is learned. Then try Find the best speaker, or headphones. The Aggressive bleed filter is the last resort.
Everything is early, or lateCalibrate again, with the speaker or headphones you're using now. On Bluetooth? There's your answer.
Extra notes right after yoursReverb or delay still on: practise dry. Otherwise it's string noise: keep Ignore quiet sounds between notes on.
Notes appear when nobody's playingSomething in the room is louder than the background. Keep Ignore background noise on (all but bass). Or lower the sensitivity a notch.
Muted strums count as notesIgnore muted string hits (Setup → 2, guitar).
“⚠ Signal too soft”A drill's way of saying it can barely hear you. Play with a sharper attack, move the phone closer, or raise the sensitivity (Setup → 2).
Fast 16ths go wrongAbove 120 BPM (200 on drums), 16th notes come too fast for the mic to tell apart; drills warn you. Slow down, or play 8ths.

Before you blame the app: five quick checks

  1. 1Is the mic ON (green)? On the Click and Train pages, Start doesn't switch it on for you.
  2. 2Any red line under the top bar? It's telling you exactly what's missing.
  3. 3Is the Instrument right, and for bass, Through an amp or Unplugged?
  4. 4Effects off? A dry sound, no reverb, no delay.
  5. 5Phone 30–60 cm away, mic side towards you, not on the amp?
💡TipMoved the phone, the room or the headphones? Calibrate again. Thirty seconds now saves an evening of “but I was on time!”
🤓Geek cornerNot sure the mic hears you at all? Setup → Diagnostics: switch the mic on and clap. Every clap should bump the onset count.

Chapter 10 · Questions and answers

You asked

The things everyone asks in week one, answered before you have to ask.

Q Does it record me?
No. It listens only while the mic is on, works out your timing on the phone as the sound arrives, and never records or saves any audio. The app has no internet access at all.
Q Amp, unplugged or headphones?
All three work. Acoustic or unplugged: just play. Through an amp: a dry sound, and the phone where it can hear the amp clearly. Headphones: wired ones, calibrated with an earbud against the mic (Chapter 2).
Q Can I keep my reverb on?
For practice, no. Reverb, delay and other effects hide timing problems and can fool the mic into hearing notes that aren't there. Turn them back on when the audience (cousin, parents, gecko) arrives.
Q Chords and strums: one note or six?
One. A strum counts from where it starts. Strum crisply: a slow, lazy strum smears its own start, and the app can only judge what it can hear.
Q Other instruments?
GROOVE GAGE is built and tuned for guitar, bass, piano and drums. Anything else with a sharp start to each note may get along with Guitar. Instruments that swell in, like bowed strings or voices, won't: the app listens for the moment a note starts.
Q Why the warning about 16ths above 120 BPM?
At 120 BPM, 16th notes are only 125 ms apart. Any faster and they come too close together for the mic to tell apart reliably. Drum hits are short and sharp, so drum drills go up to 200 BPM (75 ms apart).
Q “It says I'm late, and I'm not.”
Maybe! Calibrate first, with the speaker or headphones you're using right now. Still late? Chapter 9. Still late after that? Then, gently: maybe you are. That's what it's for.
Q Phone or tablet?
Both. On a big screen held sideways, the controls sit on the left and the lights and buttons on the right.
Q No signal in the rehearsal room?
No problem. GROOVE GAGE never needs the internet.
Q New phone?
Your sessions and settings live on the phone (Android's own backup may bring them along). Either way, run the guided setup again on the new one: every phone's speakers, mics and delays are different.
Q What happens when the beta ends?
In its last 5 days the home screen warns you: This beta stops working in 5 days. After the last day the app shows This GROOVE GAGE beta has ended. Install the next beta over it and your sessions, drills and settings stay. Uninstall it, and they go with it.
Q iPhone?
In testing through Apple's TestFlight, with most of the app already there. Chapter 11 has what's still to come and the iPhone's own settings.

Chapter 11 · The small print

The part nobody reads

Made short enough that you might.

🔒 Privacy

The mic is used only while it's switched on, the sound is analysed on the phone as it arrives, and nothing is recorded. The app has no internet access, no account and no ads. Your sessions stay on the phone unless you export and share them yourself (plus whatever Android's own backup copies).

📱 What you need

A phone or tablet with Android 8 or newer, a microphone, and permission to use it. No internet, no sign-up.

🧪 Beta builds

A test version works for 30 days. In the last 5, a red line warns you; on the last day it says This beta stops working tonight.

Found a problem?

Tell whoever sent you the beta. Say which build (the faint line at the bottom of the home screen), what you did, what you expected and what happened instead. A screenshot, or a session exported with Export…, is worth a thousand words. Confusing bits count too: if this manual had to explain it, maybe the app should have.

On iPhone

In testing through Apple's TestFlight. Most of this manual applies to it; here's how far it's got.

Already thereStill to come

The iPhone's own settings in Setup → 1 · Microphone & speaker

MicrophoneAutomatic (iOS chooses), Bottom, beside the charging port, Front, at the top by the earpiece or Back, by the cameras.
Raw mic soundOn to start: iOS leaves the mic's sound as it is instead of evening out its level. The speakers then play much quieter, so GROOVE GAGE turns the click up; the volume may need turning up too.
Click speakerBoth speakers, Bottom speaker only or Top speaker only. One speaker alone keeps the click away from the mic: the bottom one for the front or back mic, the top one for the bottom mic. It needs Raw mic sound on.
Screen upside downFor an iPhone lying with its top towards you, so the front and back mics (both up there) face you and your instrument. The screen turns to read the right way up.

Changed the mic, Raw mic sound, the click speaker or the click sound? Calibrate again: until you do, Setup says Not learned yet… in red. Test versions also have Setup → Diagnostics, where a Timing check records your next session's sound with what the app heard, and Send… shares it with whoever sent you the test.

Chapter 11 · The small print, continued

Glossary

Accent
A stronger click. Beat 1 always gets one; odd meters accent the start of each group too.
Average (avg)
Where your notes land on the whole, in ms. + is late, − is early.
BPM
Beats per minute: the tempo. Quarter notes in x/4 meters, eighth notes in x/8.
Calibration
Measuring how late the phone plays and hears sound, so only your timing gets judged.
Clean bar
A bar in which every note you played was on time.
Click bleed
The click leaking into the mic, where it could pass for a note. The smart click filter deals with it.
Count-in
One or two bars of clicks before Train or a drill starts. Not judged.
Dragging
Playing late, behind the click. Blue.
Dry sound
Your instrument with no reverb, delay or other effects. The sound to practise with.
Level
How close to the click counts as on time: Amateur ±40 ms, Seasoned ±25, Pro ±12, or Custom.
ms
Millisecond: a thousandth of a second. A blink takes 100 to 400.
Muted string hit
A strum on strings the other hand mutes: a percussive “chk” with no note. Guitar players can have them ignored.
On-time window
The ± range around the click that counts as on time: your level.
The pocket
That place just right in time where everything grooves. Where GROOVE GAGE wants you to live.
Rate me
16 bars of anything that set your level and say where you stand among players (Setup → 3).
Rushing
Playing early, ahead of the click. Red.
Spread
How much your notes wander around their average. Smaller is steadier.
Sub-click
A quieter click on the in-between notes (8ths, triplets, 16ths…).
Swing
Playing the “&” late, for that lilt. 50 % is straight, 67 % triplet swing.

Licences

Setup → About → Open-source licences lists what GROOVE GAGE is built with: the Kotlin standard library, kotlinx.coroutines, AndroidX (Core, Activity, Lifecycle, Room) and Jetpack Compose under the Apache License 2.0, and the Arimo font on the Start and Stop buttons under the SIL Open Font License 1.1.
